docs.text:
The beeline needed the appliance to hand over pixels, and no exposed operation could answer with anything but JSON. ExposeSpec grew a response media type; three routes followed.

Route Answers with Notes GET /documents/{id}/blob the original upload, unchanged Served as an attachment, under the uploader's own filename GET /documents/{id}/image one page, PNG page is 0-based; dpi defaults to 150 and is bounded GET /documents/{id}/region a rectangle of a page, PNG From the node's own anchor, or from explicit bounds

The bytes were always there — stored as Postgres large objects since 0.1.1 — but nothing under jmfts_core/rest/ could reach one. All three callers were task handlers.

attachment on /blob is the safe disposition, not a preference. That route serves uploaded bytes under the uploader's own content type from the appliance's own origin. An ingested .html or .svg served inline would execute in it.

/region takes one way of naming the rectangle, not two with a precedence rule. anchor=true asks for the node's own source_anchor, which is the form a client has after a search hit. page with bbox=x0,y0,x1,y1 names an explicit rectangle in PDF points. Passing both is a 400: there is no way to tell which was meant, and serving the wrong rectangle confidently is worse than serving none, because the reader cannot tell.

Omitting page on /image asks for the page this node is addressed at. A file node is the whole document, so that is page 0. Anything else — a chunk, a section — names its page through its own anchor, and a node with no anchor gets a 409 saying so rather than page 0.

docs.title: No highlight parameter, deliberately
docs.text: Burning the rectangle into the PNG would make the page uncacheable per-anchor, make the box unselectable and undismissable, and give the tree a second place where a rectangle is drawn. The overlay is one client component that takes an anchor and a rendered surface, and pdf-page, image and sheet-region all use it. Writing it three times is how three surfaces end up disagreeing about which corner the origin is in.

docs.title: 5. A .docx gets a rectangle, and the page says whose page it is
docs.text:
Office parity was the cut line and it landed. A .docx or .pptx is paginated by LibreOffice into a stored PDF, and a citation's rectangle is recovered off that.

That makes two anchors on one node, and they are two evidence rows because they are two facts with different truth conditions:

Row What it is How much to trust it source_anchor The document's own address — an ooxml element, or a source PDF's own geometry Exact render_anchor A page and a rectangle recovered from the rendition Approximate

A PdfAnchor now carries of, which is "source" or "rendition". It defaults to "source", and that is not laziness: every anchor written before this release is a source document's own geometry, and a default that says so is the only reading under which an old row and a new one parse alike.

\"Page 3\" and \"page 3 of our rendering\" are different claims

Two LibreOffice versions paginate differently, and the recovery can fail outright — in which case there is a render_anchor.unresolved row and no anchor at all. A viewer that draws the box says which of the two it has. The alternative is a reader opening the .docx in Word, finding the passage on page 4, and having no way to know why.

docs.title: Renditions are on, always, and the policy is eviction
docs.text:
Migration 023 adds document_renditions: derived bytes get their own table because the uploaded ones will not share theirs. document_blobs.document_id is UNIQUE, and migration 009 says why in its own DDL — one blob per document, a second version is a new node. A rendition is not a second version of the upload; it is derived from it.

The storage argument was measured rather than assumed. On a 2988 MB reference database the original bytes are 144 MB — 4.8% — so the upper bound, if every stored byte were an office document with a same-sized rendition, is +4.8%. So renditions are on by default and the policy for them is cache eviction rather than retention: every rendition row can be deleted and regenerated by re-running render:pdf, and no row in document_blobs can be regenerated by anything.

docs.title: LibreOffice is a system package, so it is an image
docs.text:
Two new task types, render:pdf and convert:ooxml, and a third dependency tier to run them. jmfts[convert] is the client only — unoserver — and Dockerfile.libreoffice builds something for it to talk to. JMFTS_CONVERT_URL is how a JMFTS finds one.

render:pdf is advisory, and that is the part the plan got wrong first. The original design gated the office anchor on after render:pdf, which is a claim on a COMPLETED row of an advisory task. On an appliance with no LibreOffice — the default — that stalls every office document short of settling, silently, forever. anchor:render is offered at the settling boundary instead. An appliance with no converter fails the conversion PERMANENTLY with a message naming the setting and the image that serves one; it never degrades quietly.

docs.title: 6. Two access gates that did not close
docs.text: Both are behaviour breaks and both are the reason this is a minor version.

docs.title: An edge takes write on its source
docs.text:
DocumentRepository.create_link constructed and flushed a DocumentLink with no principal check of any kind. DocumentService.create_link checked only that the body's source_id matched the id in the URL. So a principal with read-only access to a document could attach edges to it.

The rule is write on the source, read on the target, and it now applies to triples too: five TripleService write verbs took a subject document and an object document and gated neither, while the read side has been gated since 0.5.0. A triple is an edge, so asserting one takes write on its subject. Seventeen of the twenty-four cases in the new tests/test_access_triple_writes.py failed against the commit before the fix.

docs.title: Graph analytics compute over your graph, not the corpus
docs.text:
GET /graph/centrality, /graph/subtree-authority, /graph/spines and /graph/communities took no principal and consulted none. A caller with no grant read back the ids and titles of documents that are 404 for it everywhere else.

This changes numbers, not just rows

There were two possible fixes and they are different products. Filtering the returned ids leaks nothing but reports numbers derived from rows the caller cannot see. A centrality score is a property of the graph it was computed on, so that answer is a number about somebody else's corpus.

The filter went one layer down, into the vertex and title queries, so the graph itself is the caller's. A node dropping out also removes its descendants, so subtree_size and spread are computed over the part of the tree the caller can see. If you run these verbs as a principal without full grants, expect different scores than 0.5.1 gave you. They were wrong before.

There is now a standing audit: a test that every @expose'd verb is principal-scoped or explicitly listed. It found eleven more gaps on its first run, and step 35 — the triple write gate above — was added to the sprint because of it.

docs.title: 7. A workbook's rows reach its own index
docs.text:
index:bm25 named three prose rungs in after_any and did not name structure:sheets, and it required a text layer. So a spreadsheet was absent from its own index and from universal. On the reference corpus that read as zero index:bm25 tasks anywhere in a 21-workbook subtree, while 4,601 record nodes under it carried text averaging 457 characters.

index:bm25 is now planned at the settling boundary. The entry condition was a test written first and run against the tree before any fix: ingest one workbook under an indexed folder, drain the queue, search BM25 for a string that is in a cell.

docs.title: 8. EXPLAIN says how many, not only which
docs.text:
The ingest plan could list the rungs a format would run and could not say how much work that was. A forty-sheet workbook's profile:sheet read as one task beside structure:sheets.

The plan now folds a cost: tasks, child nodes, embeddings and LLM calls. Every accumulator returns an interval, because a fan-out atom declares a bound rather than a number, and the top of an interval is allowed to be open. PlanCost.unmeasured names what could not be counted and why — an unmeasurable count is reported, never guessed.

This is what the Ingest view's "What would happen" panel displays, and it is why dropping a file there stores nothing.

docs.title: 9. A collection configures what is ingested under it
docs.text:
GET and PUT /documents/{id}/ingest-options write an options row onto a node, and upload walks up the ancestors to find one.

A collection is not a scope a table has to express. It is a subtree, and a setting on a node reaches the documents beneath it. So this adds no bindings table and no migration — the tree is already there, and access control, already subtree-scoped, answers "who may configure this collection" with "who may write to this node", for free.

docs.title: Upgrading
docs.text:
One migration, 023_document_renditions.sql. It is additive.

jmfts-init-db --pending     # ask the database which shipped deltas it has not applied

That command has existed since 0.5.0, and schema_migrations (migration 017) is what it reads. If you are coming from 0.3.0 you have 017 through 023 to apply, and 022 swaps the token index from IVFFlat to HNSW — see the Changelog.

Read Two access gates that did not close before upgrading a multi-principal deployment. Nothing fails at deploy time; calls that used to succeed start returning 403, which is the point.

docs.title: What is not here
docs.text:
• The specifications are still held back. INGEST_SPEC.md, SPRINT_JOBS.md and OFFICE_SPEC.md are cited by several hundred source comments and are not in the public repository yet. docs/SPRINT_0_6_0.md is, and so are the generated reference pages.
  • The sprint plans and the archive are staying internal, and that is now a decision rather than a backlog item. The citations that name them dangle permanently.
  • No text-span search within a node's rectangle. Asking "where in this node's region does this phrase sit" is a real capability and it is simply not in this release.
  • /region serves a spreadsheet as cells, not as a picture of cells. For a sheet, JSON is the better answer, and GET /documents/{id}/cells already gives it.

docs.title: JMFTS — Tutorials
docs.text:
Action × Acquisition

Guided builds for JMFTS, from a first index to a tuned hybrid query.

Tutorials are read in order. The quickstart is the first one — it gets something running so the rest have somewhere to start from.

  1. Quickstart — stand the appliance up, put three documents in it, and run vector, BM25 and hybrid queries over them. Teaches what the tree is for and why only one of those three scores can be thresholded.
  2. Ingest a document — upload a real file and watch a queue turn it into a tree. Teaches that ingestion is asynchronous, what settled means, the three ways to see a pipeline's plan before running it, and what deduplication does to an upload you thought was new. Needs 0.1.1 or later.
  3. See a result on the page — the same shape in the browser: drop a file, read the plan before it runs, search seven ways at once, and click a hit to see the page with the answer boxed on it. Teaches what an anchor is, why a .docx has two of them, and how to check that the page is not doing anything the API did not do. Needs 0.6.0 or later.

All three were last checked against 0.8.0, where the appliance needs JMFTS_API_TOKEN set before it starts.

The third one stands on its own — it needs nothing from the first two, and it is the shortest way to see what the appliance does. Take it first if you would rather look than type.

Once these are done, the Cookbook is the place to go for one specific job — customizing chunking, choosing a summarization model, adding your own task type, or routing work to a GPU pool.

docs.title: JMFTS — Ingest a document
docs.text:
Action × Acquisition

Upload a real file and watch a queue turn it into a tree.

The quickstart had you write documents by hand, one JSON body at a time. That is not how a corpus arrives. This tutorial uploads a file and follows what happens to it — which is the part that surprises people, because almost none of it happens while you wait.

Needs 0.1.1 or later

The queued ingestion path shipped in 0.1.1. If you are on 0.1.0, upgrade:

git clone https://github.com/jmccardle/jmfts.git
cd jmfts && git checkout v0.8.0
export JMFTS_API_TOKEN="$(openssl rand -base64 32)"   # required since 0.8.0
docker compose up --build -d

If you already have a 0.1.0 database, apply migrations/008 through 025 in order. On 0.5.0 and later, jmfts-init-db --pending names exactly which of them yours is missing.

As before:

export TOKEN="$JMFTS_API_TOKEN"   # the value you started the appliance with; there is no default since 0.8.0
export API=http://localhost:8100

docs.title: 1. Ask what would happen, before it happens
docs.text:
Start with the question no other retrieval system will answer: what would you do to this file?

curl -sX POST "$API/ingest/explain" \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{"format": "text"}'

format is a detector name, not a pipeline name and not a file extension

Pass the short name probe would report: text, pdf, docx, pptx, zip. Markdown is not one of them. Nothing in the bytes separates authored markdown from a .txt file that opens with a #, so the detector reports both as text and one entry covers them.

The trap is that markdown is a valid name somewhere else — it is a pipeline on the older synchronous POST /ingest. Send it here and the request succeeds, because an unknown format is a legal question. The answer is a plan in which every row is impossible or not_applicable, which reads like "markdown is unsupported" and is really "no such format".

A second trap runs the other way: a real detector name does not promise the text gets read. xlsx is detected and probed, and no task extracts its text, so a plan asked without bytes still says conditional — see Office formats for which formats are actually read.

The response is the task plan, read out of the same declaration the scheduler works from — so the plan cannot drift from the run without the run changing too:

{"format": "text", "prober_available": true,
 "patterns_known": false, "patterns_source": "unknown", "patterns_ignored": [],
 "options": {"structure": {"chunk_strategy": "sentence_packed", "max_words": 120,
                           "min_chunk_length": 20},
             "rollup": {"max_children": 16, "penalty": 1.0, "min_segment": 3,
                        "llm_model": ""}},
 "tasks": [
   {"task": "probe", "outcome": "enqueued", "write_mode": "self",
    "requires": [], "forbids": []},
   {"task": "extract:text", "outcome": "conditional", "if_condition_holds": "enqueued",
    "write_mode": "self", "requires": ["has_text_layer"], "forbids": ["has_markup"]},
   {"task": "structure:declared", "outcome": "conditional", "if_condition_holds": "enqueued",
    "write_mode": "children", "after": ["extract:text"],
    "requires": ["has_text_layer", "has_headings"], "forbids": []},
   {"task": "structure:inferred", "outcome": "conditional", "if_condition_holds": "enqueued",
    "write_mode": "children", "after": ["extract:text"],
    "requires": ["has_text_layer"], "forbids": ["has_headings"]}
 ]}

Read patterns_source first. It says unknown, and patterns_known is false: this format has a prober, nobody supplied any measurements, and so most rows came back conditional. That is the honest answer to a question asked without a file. Each conditional row names the patterns that would decide it — structure:declared needs has_headings, structure:inferred refuses it — rather than guessing, because a plan resting on a fabricated input is a wrong answer wearing a confident shape.

docs.title: Three ways to ask, not two
docs.text:
There are two ways to make those rows concrete. The first supplies the patterns as a hypothesis — still no file:

curl -sX POST "$API/ingest/explain" \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{"format": "text", "patterns": {"has_text_layer": true, "has_headings": true}}'

Now patterns_source reads supplied, patterns_known is true, and every row is decided: extract:text and structure:declared are enqueued, structure:inferred is not_applicable because it forbids the heading pattern the other one requires. This is how you ask "what happens to a scanned PDF" without owning one. A key no condition consults comes back in patterns_ignored instead of being rejected, which is what makes a misspelled pattern visible rather than silently planned as false.

The second gives it the actual bytes:

curl -sX POST "$API/ingest/analyze" \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" \
  -F "file=@README.md"

analyze runs the same two pure functions probe runs, hands the result to the same planner, and stores nothing. Nothing is created, nothing is enqueued. Its plan reads patterns_source: "probed" — measured, not assumed — and it wraps the plan in three things explain cannot know:

  • file — what the bytes are, beside what your client claimed they were. mime_agrees is null rather than false when one side is unknown, because "they disagree" and "we cannot compare" are different answers.
  • probe_failed — set when probe would raise. Check it first: plan is then null, and that null means "these bytes have no schedule", not "there is nothing to do".
  • already_stored — set when this appliance already holds these bytes. An upload would resolve to that node and run no plan at all.

So: explain for a format, explain with patterns for a hypothesis, analyze for a file. This is the endpoint set to reach for when a file is behaving unexpectedly.

The plan is the downward pass only

Every row above builds the tree on the way down. The rungs that run on the way back up — summarize, summarize:llm, structure:semantic — are not in the plan and never will be. Nothing can schedule them from a format name: they are decided by the settling walk, which re-reads the tree after the children exist, because a node's rollup depends on children that do not exist yet when probe runs.

docs.title: 2. Upload it
docs.text:
curl -sX POST "$API/ingest/file" \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" \
  -F "file=@README.md"

Note the returned document id as $DOC.

Read the response carefully: it comes back almost immediately, and it does not mean your document is ingested. It means the bytes are stored and one probe task is queued. A worker does everything after that.

Uploading the same bytes twice gives you one file record, not two — the path is idempotent on content, and was_existing: true in the response says which happened. Three consequences of that are worth learning now rather than from a confusing result later.

Re-uploading with different options is refused. The existing node records the options it was ingested with. An upload asking for anything else gets a 400 naming both sets, because the alternative — returning the node as though your new max_words had been applied — is a quiet wrong answer. Changing how an already-ingested file was processed has no path today; see step 6.

Uploading into a folder links, it does not copy — or reparent. Pass parent_id for bytes that are already stored and the existing node is attached to that parent by a contains graph edge, with linked_into_parent: true in the response. Its parent_id is unchanged, so GET /documents/{parent}/subtree does not reach it and GET /documents/{parent}/links does. That is the honest cost of placing a file in two trees without duplicating its bytes, and it is worth knowing before an apparently empty folder listing sends you looking for a bug.

An upload with no parent_id is governed by nothing. Subtree RBAC works strictly on the tree path, so a node with no ancestor sits under no access-control root — and a grant made later cannot reach back and cover it. Both fixes are available only at upload time: give it a parent_id inside a subtree that is already governed, or pass ?private=true to make the new node its own access-control root with you as its only grantee. The open default is deliberate — a token means the shared knowledgebase — but this is the one gap it leaves.

docs.title: 3. Watch the frontier
docs.text:
curl -s -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" "$API/ingest/file/$DOC/frontier"

{"document_id": 41, "settled": "in_flight", "nodes_total": 9,
 "nodes_settled": 6, "nodes_in_flight": 3, "nodes_failed": 0,
 "tasks_unfinished": 4}

Run it a few times. Nodes move from in_flight to settled as the tree is built from the top down and then rolled back up.

Notice what this endpoint does not return: a percentage. The task set below the current frontier does not exist until the frontier reaches it — the pipeline discovers work as it goes — so any denominator would move backward while you watched it. Counts are the honest answer.

tasks_unfinished counts the queued tasks under this root that still owe work — pending, claimed, running, or failed-but-retryable. It is there for one specific reading: zero unfinished tasks while nodes_in_flight is above zero means the frontier is waiting on something that is not in the queue. Nothing is going to arrive and finish those nodes.

Be careful about what the other readings do not tell you. A non-zero tasks_unfinished says work is queued; it does not say anything is running it. Tasks that sit pending forever — the shape a badge with no matching worker produces — count exactly the same as tasks a worker is draining right now. Two readings a minute apart distinguish them and one reading never does: if the counts have not moved, nothing is working.

When settled reads settled, ingestion is done. If it reads failed, one of its tasks failed permanently, and that is deliberately visible rather than silent.

docs.title: 4. Look at what you got
docs.text:
curl -s -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" "$API/documents/$DOC/subtree"

The file became a tree: a file node at the top, section nodes under it following the document's own headings, and chunk nodes under those. That shape came from structure:declared — the rung that builds the tree the document declares. A document that declares no structure gets structure:inferred instead, which chunks it.

Take a section node's id out of that subtree, and ask what the pipeline knows about it:

NODE=<a section node id from the subtree above>
curl -s -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" "$API/documents/$NODE/evidence"

{"document_id": 42,
 "evidence": {"effective_content": {"method": "concatenated", "source_children": 4,
                                    "tokens": 812, "window": 8192, "characters": 4103}}}

Changed in 0.3.0. On 0.2.1 and earlier, read the node's structured_content instead.

Every name the pipeline writes about a node — matched.patterns, effective_content, the attempt log, twenty-nine in all — used to live in documents.structured_content beside whatever the caller had put there. 0.3.0 moved them to their own table and stitched nothing back into the document response, so that column is now exactly what a caller wrote and this route is where the pipeline's own facts are.

Read a null value and a missing key as different answers: a name present with null says a task ran and produced nothing, and a name absent says nothing has run.

effective_content is a container's answer to "what do you say?". It has no content of its own — the prose lives in its leaves, and putting it on the container too would enter the same text into the indexes twice. So instead it gets an embedding derived from its children, and a record of how.

method is the thing to read. concatenated means the children's text fit the embedding window and was used verbatim. llm_summary means it did not fit and a model paraphrased it. The first is a stronger record of what the document said; the deciding token count is recorded either way so you never have to infer which happened from the text.

docs.title: 5. Search it
docs.text:
Now the tree is settled, it is searchable:

curl -sX POST "$API/search/vector" \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d "{\"query\": \"how do I run the tests\", \"parent_id\": $DOC, \"limit\": 5}"

Try that same query before a document finishes and you get nothing back. The retrieval indexes are partial on settled, so an unfinished tree is invisible. That is intended — a half-built tree should not answer queries — but it means "no results" and "still ingesting" look identical from outside. The frontier endpoint is how you tell them apart.

docs.title: 6. When something goes wrong
docs.text:
Two limits are worth knowing before you need them, because neither is obvious from the endpoints you have used so far.

There is no API for the queue. No endpoint lists task rows, shows you which one failed, or retries one. What you get is the frontier's counts and, if the appliance is yours, SQL against task_queue. For a corpus rather than a single file, scripts/e2e_ingest_corpus.py report is the tool that answers it — it lists every failed task with its error type, alongside what the trees became and what each task type cost.

There is no re-ingest. A file is processed once, with the options it was uploaded under. Changing those options for a file already in the appliance is specified — it diffs (task, param_fingerprint) against the node's attempt log and enqueues only the difference — and not built. Until it is, the only way to reprocess a document under new options is to delete it and upload it again.

So decide options before the upload, not after, and use analyze to check a file that is behaving strangely rather than uploading it to find out.

docs.title: What you learned
docs.text:
• Ingestion is asynchronous. A 200 from the upload means accepted, not ingested.
  • The plan is inspectable before it runs. explain from a format name, explain with patterns from a hypothesis, analyze from real bytes — none of the three storing anything.
  • The plan covers the way down. Rollup rungs are decided later, by a walk that re-reads the tree.
  • settled gates retrieval. Unfinished documents are invisible on purpose.
  • A container's embedding is derived and labelled. effective_content.method says whether you are searching the document's own words or a paraphrase of them.
  • Uploads deduplicate on content, which makes placement a link rather than a copy, makes conflicting options a refusal, and makes options a decision you take before uploading.

docs.title: Next
docs.text:
• Change what the pipeline does. Chunking per request and a different summarization model are both one options key — read the chunking recipe's caveat before trying it on a file you have already uploaded.
  • Do a whole directory. e2e_ingest_corpus.py handles the upload/wait/index phases and reports what happened, including every failed task.
  • File the same document in two places. Placement is a link, which a subtree walk will not show you.
  • Control who sees an upload. private=true and the ungoverned-node gap — a decision you can only make at upload time.
  • Add your own step. Register a task handler to put your own work in the pipeline.
  • Scale it out. The DevOps Manual covers running workers as their own processes, the heartbeat lease, routing work to pools by badge, and what you can monitor given there is no queue API.

docs.title: JMFTS — Quickstart
docs.text:
Action × Acquisition

Index a small corpus and run your first hybrid query.

You will stand up the appliance, put three documents in it, search them by meaning, add a BM25 index, and then run the hybrid query that uses both. Most of the time is the embedding model downloading.

Everything here has been in JMFTS since 0.1.0, and was last checked against 0.8.0. The one break in the Changelog that reaches it is the token: since 0.8.0 JMFTS_API_TOKEN has no default, so you choose one in step 1. Every request body below carries only declared fields, which 0.8.0 enforces (an undeclared field is a 422).

If you would rather look than type, See a result on the page does the same shape in the browser and needs nothing from this page.

docs.title: 1. Start it
docs.text:
git clone https://github.com/jmccardle/jmfts.git
cd jmfts
export JMFTS_API_TOKEN="$(openssl rand -base64 32)"
docker compose up --build -d
docker compose logs -f api

The first build downloads a CPU build of torch, and the first request downloads nomic-ai/modernbert-embed-base — a few hundred MB, cached in a volume so it only happens once.

The Compose file has no default for the token: it stops and says so if JMFTS_API_TOKEN is unset, and so does the server (0.8.0; before that it generated one and printed it). Use the value you exported above, and the API root:

export TOKEN="$JMFTS_API_TOKEN"
export API=http://localhost:8100

Every request needs Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN. There is no mode where a blank token means "allow all."

docs.title: 2. Put something in it
docs.text:
Documents form a tree. Make a parent so you have something to scope searches to:

curl -sX POST "$API/documents" \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{"title": "Notes", "usetype": "markdown"}'

Keep the id it returns as $ROOT, then add three children:

for t in \
  "Cosine similarity measures the angle between two vectors, ignoring magnitude." \
  "BM25 scores a document by term frequency, saturating so repeated words stop helping." \
  "The kettle needs descaling again and the good mugs are in the dishwasher."
do
  curl -sX POST "$API/documents" \
    -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
    -d "{\"parent_id\": $ROOT, \"content\": \"$t\", \"usetype\": \"markdown\"}"
done

auto_embed defaults to true, so each document was embedded as it was created — a 768-dim document vector plus per-token vectors for late interaction. That is why creates are slower than they look: embedding is roughly 100× the cost of the database write itself.

docs.title: 3. Search by meaning
docs.text:
Vector search needs no index. It reads the vectors that were written on create:

curl -sX POST "$API/search/vector" \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d "{\"query\": \"how is relevance scored\", \"parent_id\": $ROOT, \"limit\": 3}"

The two retrieval sentences come back ahead of the kettle, and none of the query's words appear in either. Look at the scores, not just the order: cosine similarity separates, so the relevant hits sit meaningfully above the irrelevant one. That property matters in step 5.

docs.title: 4. Add the keyword leg
docs.text:
BM25 needs an inverted index, and an index needs to know which subtree it covers:

curl -sX POST "$API/indexes" \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{"name": "notes", "description": "quickstart corpus"}'

curl -sX POST "$API/indexes/notes/roots" \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d "{\"root_document_id\": $ROOT}"

Then index each document you created:

curl -sX POST "$API/indexes/notes/index-document/$DOC_ID" \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN"

This is idempotent — indexing a document twice subtracts its old contribution before adding the new one, so the corpus statistics BM25's IDF is derived from do not inflate. Index incrementally as content arrives. POST /indexes/notes/refresh rebuilds from scratch and costs time proportional to the whole corpus, so reach for it as a repair tool rather than a routine one.

Now a keyword query that vector search alone would do poorly on:

curl -sX POST "$API/search/bm25" \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{"query": "BM25", "index_name": "notes", "limit": 3}'

docs.title: 5. Run the hybrid query
docs.text:
curl -sX POST "$API/search/hybrid" \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d "{\"query\": \"how is relevance scored\", \"parent_id\": $ROOT,
       \"index_name\": \"notes\", \"weights\": {\"vector\": 0.6, \"bm25\": 0.4}}"

Omit weights and you get the tuned 0.86/0.14 default. Pass an explicit {} for equal-weight RRF.

The hybrid score is not a similarity

Hybrid fuses by rank: each leg contributes weight/(60+rank). The number that comes back says where a result placed, not how similar it was. Measured against a real store, a relevant query and a nonsense query returned the same five score values.

So: rank with hybrid, threshold with vector. If anything downstream has to decide something from a score — inject this context or stay silent, keep this result or drop it — vector is the only method that answers.

docs.title: What you have
docs.text: Three documents, two ways to search them, and one fused query. The tree is what makes parent_id a scope rather than a filter, so one appliance can hold several corpora and a search can name one.

docs.title: Next
docs.text:
• Get a real corpus in. Ingest a directory — files rather than hand-written JSON, with a queue doing the tree-building. Needs 0.1.1 or later.
  • Tune what you just ran. The Cookbook has measured hybrid weightings per dataset, and why one global number does not hold.
  • Add reranking. ?rerank=true adds a second stage; the Cookbook explains why the choice is about prerequisites rather than quality.
  • Run it properly. The DevOps Manual covers auth, the embedding device, and why bulk loading stays CPU-bound until you move it to CUDA.

docs.title: JMFTS — See a result on the page
docs.text:
Action × Acquisition

Drag a PDF in, search it, click a result, and see the page with the answer boxed on it.

That sentence is the whole of 0.6.0's front end, and running it end to end takes about ten minutes once the appliance is up. You will watch an ingest plan before it runs, watch the queue settle the document, run one query down seven columns at once, and finish on a page that shows you where the answer physically sits.

Needs 0.6.0 or later

The front end is a separate distribution, jmfts-web, and jmfts[web] is what pulls it in. An appliance without it starts normally and serves no /app.

The Quickstart does the same corpus by hand with curl. Do that one if you want to know what the calls are; do this one if you want to see what they are for. Neither depends on the other.

docs.title: 1. Get an appliance with a face
docs.text:
From a checkout, the dev stack carries the front end:

git clone https://github.com/jmccardle/jmfts.git
cd jmfts && docker compose up --build -d
docker compose logs -f api

Set JMFTS_API_TOKEN first (export JMFTS_API_TOKEN="$(openssl rand -base64 32)"); since 0.8.0 compose stops without it, and you will paste the same value into the page in step 2.

If you already have JMFTS running some other way, add the front end to it:

pip install 'jmfts[web]'

And from nothing, without Docker:

python3 -m venv .venv && . .venv/bin/activate
pip install 'jmfts[embed,web]'
export JMFTS_API_TOKEN="$(openssl rand -base64 32)"
jmfts-init-db
uvicorn jmfts_core.rest.main:app --host 0.0.0.0 --port 8100

[embed] is the model stack, and it is separate for a reason worth knowing: base JMFTS carries no torch, because a storage worker can ask another appliance for vectors. The machine serving /search embeds its queries locally whatever else is configured, so it needs the model.

Then open:

http://localhost:8100/app/

docs.title: 2. Connect
docs.text:
There is one field at the top of the shell and it wants your JMFTS_API_TOKEN. Paste it and press Connect.

The status line then says connected — this browser keeps the token until you press Forget, and it means the browser, not the tab: open a second tab on the same appliance and it is already signed in. Forget is the counterweight — it signs out every tab at once.

Nothing but /health works without a token, so if the views look broken, look at that line first.

docs.title: 3. Drop a file, and read what would happen
docs.text:
Go to Ingest. Drop a PDF onto the panel.

Nothing has been stored. Dropping a file analyses it: probe runs over the bytes, and the page fills a section headed What would happen — which carries the reassurance in its subtitle, Nothing below has been stored.

Three things to read there:

  • The format, and what recognised it. Not the file extension — what the bytes say.
  • The patterns. What probe measured in the file: a text layer, tables, declared structure. Some are listed as known and unused, which is the appliance telling you it saw something it has no rung for.
  • The plan, with a cost. One row per task: the task type, the scope it runs at, whether it is conditional and on what. Since 0.6.0 each row also carries counts — tasks, child nodes, embeddings, LLM calls.

Those counts are intervals, not numbers, and some of them have an open top. A fan-out task declares a bound rather than a count, and EXPLAIN has not been given the bytes, so "between 1 and 40 profile tasks" is the honest answer and 40 would not be. Anything that could not be counted at all is named in unmeasured with the reason. This is the appliance refusing to guess at you.

docs.title: 4. Ingest it, and watch the frontier
docs.text:
Press Ingest. Now it is stored, and the queue has work.

The panel switches to the settling frontier and polls it. Five numbers, and they are worth understanding because they are the appliance's own lifecycle:

Number What it counts nodes_total Everything created under this upload so far nodes_settled Nodes whose whole subtree has finished nodes_in_flight Nodes still being worked on nodes_failed Nodes a task gave up on tasks_unfinished Queue items not yet drained

An in-flight node is invisible to search. Every retrieval index is partial on settled, which is why the page waits for the root to settle before it calls the ingest done rather than reporting success the moment the upload returned.

If nodes_total keeps climbing, that is the tree being built — a PDF becomes a file node, then sections, then chunks, each of which is a row.

docs.title: 5. One query, seven columns
docs.text:
Go to Search and type a question about something in the document.

The page runs it seven ways at once and puts the answers side by side:

Column What it is vector HNSW cosine over the 768-dim document embedding fulltext PostgreSQL ts_vector, with a trigram fallback bm25 The inverted index, k1/b tuned maxsim Late interaction over the per-token 256-dim vectors hybrid Reciprocal Rank Fusion over the first two auto A router reads the query, picks one method, and says why quick (GET) The same algorithms in a URL

This is the shortest explanation of the appliance there is. Try a question phrased in words that are not in the document — vector and maxsim will find it and bm25 will not. Then try an exact string, a surname or a part number, and watch that reverse.

Read the applied block under hybrid. The page deliberately does not tell the server which methods to fuse; it omits methods and lets the tuned default resolve, and applied reports what that came out as. A page that named a default would be a second copy of it, and would be wrong the day the default moved.

The hybrid score is not a similarity

Fusion is by rank: each leg contributes weight/(60+rank). The number says where a result placed, not how close it was. Rank with hybrid, threshold with vector.

docs.title: 6. Click a hit
docs.text:
Click a result. You land on Document, on the node that matched — and if the appliance can draw it, the page is rendered with a box around the passage.

The box comes from the hit itself. A search result carries its anchor, so the page needs no extra call per hit to know where to draw: {"kind": "pdf", "page": 3, "bbox": [...]} in PDF points, drawn by one overlay component that every surface shares.

For a .docx or .pptx there are two anchors and the page says which it is showing:

  • source_anchor is the document's own address — an element of the uploaded package. It is exact, and it cannot be drawn.
  • render_anchor is a rectangle found in the PDF LibreOffice paginated. It can be drawn, and it can be wrong: another version of LibreOffice may put the passage on a different page.

The page's own sentence for that case is the rule worth keeping: cite the address; look at the rectangle.

When there is no box, the page tells you which of four reasons it is — the passage has an exact address and nothing has paginated the document; a rendition exists and the passage was not found in it, with the reason; and so on. "No highlight" and "the highlight could not be recovered" are different answers, and only one of them is a problem.

docs.title: 7. Check that the page is thin
docs.text:
Go to Call log.

Every request any view made is there: operation id, method, resolved path, params, body, status, elapsed milliseconds. Three things you can do with it, and the third is the reason it exists:

  1. Replay an event with edited arguments, and see the response render properly rather than as a blob.
  2. Audit the page. Anything a view showed that has no call behind it was computed in the browser. You can see that here rather than take it on trust.
  3. Copy out. Any event prints as curl, as a RemoteJmftsClient call, or as fetch — and none of the three prints your token. Each names the environment variable it lives in.

Point 3 is how this tutorial connects to the Quickstart: run something on the page, copy it out as curl, and you have the hand-written form of the thing you just clicked.

docs.title: What you have
docs.text: One document, ingested with its plan shown first, searched seven ways, and a rectangle on a page. The whole front end is ES modules over the same REST API any other client calls — nothing loads from a CDN or a font host, because an appliance is expected to run air-gapped.

docs.title: Next
docs.text:
• Save what you just ran. The Presets view stores a search configuration as a search context and runs it again later.
  • Ask the appliance what it is. This appliance is GET /capabilities — which extras are installed, whether it can embed at all, which formats it identifies, which methods will actually return something here.
  • Do it by hand. The Quickstart builds a small corpus with curl and explains what each call is doing.
  • Put a real corpus in. Ingest a document covers the queue, the task types, and where a rung records what it did.

docs.title: Tau
docs.text:
Tau is a hackable coding agent harness for CLI, TUI, REPL, or RPC. Extensions are Python. A session is a tree you can branch; context is a walk of it.

Which Tau

This section documents the stable v0.15.0 release (Python, pip install ffwf-tau). An unreleased Rust rewrite, 0.16 "Trusty", is documented under the 0.16 preview.

Everything reaches Tau through one methodTau sits at the centre as a rounded pill labelled AgentSession. Five inputs converge on it from the left — a Tectum agent node named agent dot persona underscore reflection, the tau TUI, tau dash p, the SDK's create underscore agent underscore session, and an extension's api dot submit — and every one lands on the same red bar marked submit before a single arrow enters the session. Above, a Tectum subject rail feeds the agent node, and a second rail carries the session's speak tool back out onto the bus. To the right the spine continues past the pill, forks at a filled dot, and splits into a solid branch that extends the active leaf and a dashed one left behind as an abandoned sibling. Below, two hatched slabs are the two places a session can be stored: a plain slab for a JSONL file under tilde slash dot tau slash sessions, and a doubled JMFTS slab where each entry becomes a document alongside the rest of the corpus.events.sensation.audio.filteredevents.workspace.persona_reflection.out.speakagent.persona_reflectiontautau -pcreate_agent_sessionapi.submit()submit()one doorAgentSessionextends the leafabandoned siblingtool: speak--store file--store jmfts~/.tau/sessionsevery input sourcea JSONL file per sessiondocumentstau:conversationan entry is a documentEverything that can drive Tau — a Tectum agent node holding the session open over RPC, the TUI, a headless run, the SDK, an extension — arrives at the same method. What comes back out is a tree rather than a log: the spine forks, and a rollback leaves the abandoned branch on disk instead of deleting it. The substrate above hears the turn's result as an ordinary event. The store below is a flag, and pointing it at JMFTS files every entry as a document beside the rest of the corpus.

docs.title: Install
docs.text:
pip install ffwf-tau

Then run tau. It needs Python 3.12 or newer. The meta package pulls in the TUI; the bare ffwf-tau-coding-agent package is CLI and RPC only. The ffwf- prefix is required — tau-ai and tau on PyPI are unrelated projects. The DevOps Manual covers the extras and the second command name.

Out of the box τ talks to any OpenAI-compatible endpoint, local or hosted. Anthropic and Google are two more wire protocols, behind the extras ffwf-tau-llm[anthropic] and ffwf-tau-llm[google]. The ffwf-tau meta package installs both; the SDKs import only when a model actually names them.

docs.title: Where to start
docs.text:
The four categories below are a crosswalk, not a sequence. Pick the cell you are actually in.

Acquisition Application Action Tutorials Action × Acquisition

Guided builds. Concepts as you go, quickstart first.

Cookbook Action × Application

Recipes for one job. Step by step.

Cognition DevOps Manual Cognition × Acquisition

Deployment, operation, and why it's like that.

Reference Cognition × Application

API, config, schemas. Unfiltered lookup by module or endpoint.

docs.title: Tau — Cookbook
docs.text:
Action × Application

Recipes for specific Tau jobs — writing an extension, branching a session, storing state in the tree, supervising a fleet, pointing the TUI at a different backend. Each one is drawn from an example or script that ships in the source tree (checked against v0.15.0); the cited file is always the working version.

docs.title: Give the model a new tool
docs.text:
Three pieces, and api.register_tool wants all of them in one dict. From examples/05_custom_tool.py, the smallest complete version:

def greet_execute(tool_call_id, params, signal, on_update, ctx):
    return {"content": [{"type": "text", "text": f"Hello, {params['name']}!"}]}

GREET_TOOL = {
    "name": "greet",
    "label": "Greet",
    "description": "Greet someone by name.",
    "parameters": {
        "type": "object",
        "properties": {"name": {"type": "string", "description": "Who to greet."}},
        "required": ["name"],
    },
    "execute": greet_execute,          # required — see below
    "execution_mode": "sequential",
}

def register(api):
    api.register_tool(GREET_TOOL)

The parameters JSON Schema is what the model reads to decide how to call the tool, and what τ validates every call against. execute takes five arguments and may be sync or async; τ awaits it either way. The result dict becomes the toolResult message the model reads on its next turn — add "is_error": True to tell it the call failed.

Two things bite here, and both did in this repo's own examples until they were caught by a contract test. execute is a required key, so defining the function and forgetting to put it in the dict raises ValueError: register_tool: missing required key 'execute' at load. And register is the only name the file-path loader looks up — a conventionally-named greet_tool_extension is not a substitute, and tau -e will raise AttributeError on a module without it.

examples/03_dynamic_env_tool.py is the same shape with the two things a real tool needs: it redacts values that look like credentials, and it bounds its own output so a large environment cannot flood the context window.

docs.title: Know which handler signature you need
docs.text:
τ has two event vocabularies and they take different handlers. Getting this wrong fails at dispatch time — which for session_shutdown means at the very end of a session, and for tool_call means the handler raises, which as of 0.15 ends the turn.

Kind Names Handler event is notify all, agent_start, message_update, tool_execution_end, … handler(event) an AgentEvent object — attributes hook tool_call, tool_result, input, before_agent_start, turn_end, user_turn_end, session_before_switch, annotate, entry_written, turn_setting_changed, and the lifecycle pair session_start and session_shutdown handler(event, ctx) a plain dict

api.on(name, handler) routes by name, so you do not choose — the name you subscribe to decides which contract you owe. Hooks can change the run (block a call, patch arguments, append a durable message); notify events cannot, and their return value is ignored.

A raising handler is not harmless any more. At input, before_agent_start, tool_call, tool_result, turn_end, user_turn_end, session_before_switch and annotate, an exception ends the turn: agent_end carries end_reason: "error" naming your extension and the hook, and prompt() raises HookHandlerError. At entry_written, turn_setting_changed and the lifecycle hooks the error is reported and the turn goes on. Catch what your handler can recover from; an extension that enforces a rule should stop enforcing it only on purpose.

The turn-boundary pair is the other easy mistake: turn_end fires once per agent-loop turn, so one request resolved in six tool round-trips fires it six times. user_turn_end fires once per prompt() — once per thing the user actually asked for. examples/02_git_checkpoint.py uses the latter, because six commits for one request is not a checkpoint.

docs.title: Veto a dangerous tool call before it runs
docs.text:
The tool_call hook is the one hook that can actually block execution — a notify-only event's return value is ignored, so subscribing to tool_execution_start instead (an earlier version of this exact demo did) prints a warning and then lets the destructive command run anyway. The real shape, from the source tree's examples/01_permission_gate.py:

import re

BLOCKED_PATTERNS = [
    r"\brm\s+-rf\s+/",
    r"\bchmod\s+777",
    r"\bdd\s+",
    r"\bmkfs\b",
    r">\s*/dev/(sd|vd|nvme)",
]
COMPILED_PATTERNS = [re.compile(p) for p in BLOCKED_PATTERNS]

def permission_gate_tool_call(event, ctx):
    if event["tool_name"] != "bash":
        return None
    command = str(event.get("input", {}).get("command") or "")
    for pattern in COMPILED_PATTERNS:
        if pattern.search(command):
            return {
                "block": True,
                "reason": f"Denied: matches destructive pattern {pattern.pattern!r}",
            }
    return None

def register(api):
    api.on("tool_call", permission_gate_tool_call)

Returning {"block": True, "reason": ...} from a tool_call handler turns into an error tool result the model reacts to — it does not silently swallow the call. Load it directly: tau -e examples/01_permission_gate.py (naming it with -e authorizes it; an extension merely found in <τ home>/extensions or in an installed package loads only once tau ext authorize has recorded it). The human-in-the-loop variant is examples/30_permission_gate.py: it asks with api.request_user_action rather than a modal, so the question is an entry on the session and every head can answer it. A config-driven path denylist is examples/31_protected_paths.py.

docs.title: Bridge a session onto a NATS bus (Tectum integration)
docs.text:
nats_bus.py (tau-006/tau-007; shipped as a built-in under tau_agent_core.extensions_builtin) lets τ speak NATS directly — subscribing an inbound subject to drive turns, and registering one tool per outbound verb (speak, journal_append, jmfts_write, delegate, plus world verbs for a simulation engine: move_to, wait, note). Its NATS client is an extra rather than a base dependency — pip install 'ffwf-tau-agent-core[bus]' — and it requires an explicit capability grant on top of that, because it declares TOUCHES_BUS = True:

from tau_agent_core.sdk import create_agent_session

session = create_agent_session(
    model=my_model,
    tools=[],
    system_prompt=SYSTEM_PROMPT,
    bus_available=True,   # required — a TOUCHES_BUS extension is refused without it
)

result = await session.load_extensions(
    [str(nats_bus_path)],
    discover=False,
    extensions_config={
        "nats_bus": {
            "workspace": "responder",                             # required
            "inbound_subject": "events.sensation.audio.resolved.clean",  # required
            "nats_url": "nats://127.0.0.1:4222",
            "verbs": ("speak", "journal_append"),
        }
    },
)

workspace and inbound_subject have no defaults on purpose — a guessed workspace publishes to the wrong subject, and a guessed inbound subject silently never fires. The full working version of this, including CLI args and a real llama.cpp model config, is scripts/tectum_responder.py in the source tree — read it over hand-adapting the snippet above, since it is the one thing this extension is actually exercised end to end against.

The wire format (the TectumEvent envelope, subject naming, ack shapes) is shared with Tectum's own docs — see the Tectum + Tau integration page.

docs.title: Fork a session instead of extending it
docs.text:
ctx.fork(entry_id=None, mode="in_place") branches the conversation off a point in the tree without touching the source log — the next turn appends a new sibling branch rather than continuing the active leaf:

async def fork_handler(event, ctx):
    # Branch off the current leaf (entry_id=None), staying in the same file.
    await ctx.fork(mode="in_place")

mode="export" instead copies the whole session into a new file via the file-backed store's own fork — useful for "try an alternative from here without touching the session someone is actively looking at." It raises on an in-memory (SDK) log, which cannot be exported to a file — there is no silent degrade to an in-place fork instead.

A spawned child branch (ctx.spawn_branch) can start with messages already written on it (seed=[…]), and runs the extension hooks by default.

For undoing a turn rather than branching from it, AgentSession.submit()'s multitask_strategy="rollback" navigates back to the pre-turn leaf; the turn that gets rolled back becomes an abandoned sibling branch, not a deletion — nothing in a Tau session is destroyed by a rollback. In the TUI this is Ctrl+Z.

docs.title: Keep state in the tree, not beside it
docs.text:
The obvious way to give an agent a todo list is a JSON file next to the session. examples/38_todo.py does it with no side database at all: every mutation the tool performs writes the new list snapshot as a durable customEntry node, and a read reconstructs the list from the latest snapshot on the active path. customEntry nodes are excluded from the model's context by kind, so this costs no tokens — the model sees the list only when the tool shows it.

The payoff is that the state inherits every property of the tree, for free:

  • Ctrl+Z rolls back a turn — and the todo mutations from that turn vanish with it, because they hang off the abandoned branch.
  • Fork the session and each branch carries its own divergent list.
  • Reload, resume, or export the session and the list comes along, because there is nothing beside the session to lose.

ext_kit/state.py ships TreeStore, the generic replaying wrapper, for any extension state that should time-travel with the conversation instead of outliving it in a stale file.

docs.title: Ask one model for a dozen verdicts, one forward pass each
docs.text:
ctx.complete() is stateless — no tree writes, no cursor movement — so it is safe under asyncio.gather at any fan-out. Combine that with DecodeConstraints(choices=[...]) and a classification over N candidates becomes N concurrent calls, each pinned to a label set so tightly that on a llama.cpp/llguidance backend a verdict costs about one forward pass:

from tau_llm.constraints import DecodeConstraints

constraints = DecodeConstraints(choices=["supported", "contradicted", "unrelated"])

examples/60_retrieval_review.py is the working version: it takes real retrieval hits and scores every one concurrently against a claim. Three contract details matter, all enforced at construction or at the boundary:

  • Exactly one of grammar / json_schema / choices may be set.
  • A hand-written grammar= string must also carry verify= — a callable that checks the output actually conforms. τ will not reimplement a grammar engine to check a grammar it did not build, and it will not report a constraint held when it cannot tell. Build the grammar with tau_llm.grammar (choice/fixed/regex/sequence, each of which carries its own checker) and the verifier comes with it; choices=[...] needs nothing extra.
  • If the server's output somehow escapes the declared constraint, τ raises ConstraintViolation rather than returning it — a grammar that died mid-generation produces fabricated data, and fabricated data is a fault, not a near miss.

The second and third are the same rule at two moments: a constraint nobody can check is indistinguishable from no constraint at all.

docs.title: Supervise a fleet from inside a session
docs.text:
The sanctioned isolated-child invocation is:

tau -p --mode json --no-session --no-extensions

— fully ephemeral, unhookable, machine-readable. examples/51_delegate_fleet.py builds a /fleet command on it: read-only children fan out over subtasks while the parent session paints a live dashboard with ctx.ui.panel — and because panel actions dispatch registered commands back into the extension, the dashboard is a control surface, not a report: you can steer a running child from the panel mid-flight.

Panels are not TUI-only. In headless --mode json they serialize onto the event stream as {"type": "extension", "kind": "panel", ...}, so a parent process reading a child's stream sees the child's dashboard and its declared actions. A τ supervising τs that supervise their own children is the same recipe applied twice; ext_kit/spawn.py and ext_kit/stream.py provide the pool, limits, and stuck-detection so the outer layer notices when an inner one stalls.

docs.title: Wrap a built-in tool without forking it
docs.text:
Extension tools resolve after built-ins, so registering a tool named bash shadows the built-in bash for the model. ext_kit/steer.py ships wrap_tool on exactly this mechanism: keep the original schema, delegate to the original implementation, and add before/after hooks with a short-circuit veto.

This is a different altitude than the tool_call hook. The hook sees every tool call and can block or patch arguments before execution; a wrapper owns one tool's whole call — it can rewrite the input, run the real tool, transform the result, or answer without running it at all. Audit logs, dry-run modes, per-directory sandboxes, and result redaction all land here, with no changes to the harness and no fork of the tool.

docs.title: Let the outside world join the conversation
docs.text:
examples/36_file_trigger.py starts a background watcher on session_start; when the watched file changes, the extension calls api.send_user_message(content) and the change becomes a conversational turn. The same shape works for anything that can wake a coroutine — a timer, a webhook, an MQTT topic, a mailbox.

deliver_as picks the urgency: "followUp" runs after the current turn, "nextTurn" parks until the next submission, and "steer" delivers into the already running turn, after its current tool calls and before its next model call. And provenance is unforgeable by construction: the runtime stamps source="extension" and the extension's own name as submitter, and neither is a parameter — the transcript can never claim a machine-made message came from the human.

docs.title: Hand the model the scissors
docs.text:
examples/23_context_surgeon.py registers session-control tools — compact now, fork from here, summarize that branch — built on ctx.compact(), ctx.fork(), and ctx.summarize_branch() with defer=True. The deferral is the recipe: a tool that restructured the context mid-turn would saw off the branch the model is standing on, so the intent is recorded when the tool runs and applied exactly once at the tail of the submission.

The result is an agent that manages its own context window as a matter of policy — noticing via ctx.get_context_usage() that it is running long and compacting itself, or forking a clean continuation when the task changes shape — instead of waiting for a human to notice on its behalf. examples/39_trigger_compact.py is the fully automatic edge-triggered variant; examples/40_handoff.py is the same idea aimed forward: summarize, fork, and hand the work to a focused successor session.

docs.title: Drop the old history without deleting it
docs.text:
Compaction replaces a span with an LLM-written summary. Its blunter cousin is elide: a summary-less splice anchor that folds the old history out of the model's context. Nothing is erased — everything stays on disk and in the tree, and navigation can walk back into it — but the fold skips it, so the model no longer pays for it.

In the TUI this is Ctrl+E inside the Ctrl+G tree browser. Read the line under the tree before you press it, because the two ends bracket what is kept, not what is removed: over [1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6], pairing 2 with 4 leaves [2, 3, 4], and cutting a span out of the middle is not something the operation can express. The ordinary case is one keystroke: put the cursor on the oldest entry you want to keep and press Ctrl+E. To choose both ends, mark one with Space, move to the other, and press Ctrl+E; the tree decides which is which. If the deeper end is not the current tip, the conversation moves back to it and the newer entries leave the context too, which the line says first.

It is the honest tool for the case where a summary would add nothing: a hundred turns of test-and-fix noise whose only useful residue is the final green run. You chose the cut; no model invented a summary of what was cut. docs/TREE-EDITOR-MANUAL.md in the source tree has the full manual, including Ctrl+B (branch from the marked rows, keeping a selection with gaps) and c / v (copy and paste a subtree).

docs.title: Point the TUI at a different session backend
docs.text:
--store jmfts swaps the file-backed session store for a JMFTS-backed one — useful when a deployment wants sessions to be searchable the same way a JMFTS-indexed document corpus is, rather than plain files on disk:

tau --store jmfts
tau -p --store jmfts "..."

--import-session x.jsonl copies a file session into the JMFTS store and --export-session REF x.jsonl copies one back; tau --export-html REF renders either as a single HTML page.

ffwf-tau-jmfts is an optional package (pip install 'ffwf-tau-coding-agent[jmfts]'), loaded lazily only when --store jmfts (or the equivalent config key) selects it — never a hard dependency of the TUI or CLI. See the Tau + JMFTS integration page for what that buys an agent beyond session storage.

docs.title: Tau — DevOps Manual
docs.text:
Cognition × Acquisition

How Tau is deployed and operated: where sessions live, how model credentials are supplied, and where the boundary between harness and agent actually falls.

Draft

Written from the source repo's own README and design docs, and checked against the v0.15.0 source and a v0.15.0 install. Not yet checked against a deployment outside the maintainer's own.

docs.title: Install
docs.text:
pip install ffwf-tau                          # the meta package: CLI, RPC, TUI, all three wires
pip install ffwf-tau-coding-agent             # headless only: CLI and RPC

Python 3.12 or newer is required. 0.15.0 dropped 3.11; the release matrix runs 3.12, 3.13, 3.14 and the free-threaded 3.14t and 3.15t builds, and the project gates on no module re-enabling the GIL. All five distributions are on PyPI at 0.15.0.

The meta package is the guessable name and ships no code. It depends, all at the same version, on ffwf-tau-coding-agent[tui], ffwf-tau-agent-core[images] and ffwf-tau-llm[anthropic,google], so a bare ffwf-tau speaks all three wire protocols and reads screenshots. It deliberately does not pull [jmfts] (that store needs a running server) or the daemon (ffwf-tau[serve] adds that). The base distribution pulls ffwf-tau-agent-core and ffwf-tau-llm behind it. [tui] adds Textual and Rich, and that extra is the only thing an interactive tau needs that a headless one does not — without it, tau -p and tau --mode rpc still run a full turn, extensions and all. Measured: 15 packages and 13 MB against 27 packages and 31 MB. That gap is the argument for the split, because a container that only ever runs headless turns has no reason to ship a terminal interface.

The other capabilities are extras on the same principle — [repl] for --mode repl, [jmfts] for --store jmfts, [serve] for tau serve and --connect, ffwf-tau-agent-core[bus] for the nats_bus extension. Each reports its own absence with the install command rather than a traceback. The Reference page carries the full table.

The ffwf- prefix is load-bearing rather than branding: tau-ai and tau on PyPI are unrelated third-party projects, so an install command missing the prefix installs someone else's code.

docs.title: Which command name to write
docs.text: The install puts both tau and ffwf-tau on PATH — one entry point, two wrappers pip owns and removes on uninstall. Type tau at a terminal; write ffwf-tau in a systemd unit, a Dockerfile, or a cron line. PyPI reserves distribution names but not command names, and an unrelated project ships its own tau: in an environment holding both, whichever installed last owns the name, and nothing tells you which one that was. ffwf-tau cannot be taken.

docs.title: Ways to run τ
docs.text:
Mode Entry point Shape Interactive tau Textual TUI in a terminal. Headless print tau -p "..." One turn, prints a transcript, exits. Headless JSON tau -p --mode json "..." One turn, JSONL lifecycle events instead of text — the machine-readable equivalent of the TUI's stream. RPC subprocess tau --mode rpc A persistent JSON-RPC 2.0 server over stdio — τ as a process a host drives, not a library it imports. See the Reference page for the verb table. REPL tau --mode repl An interactive prompt line in the terminal's own scrollback, no screen takeover. Behind the [repl] extra (rich renders, prompt_toolkit reads); needs no Textual. Daemon tau serve A WebSocket server that owns sessions (default 127.0.0.1:8256, or unix:/PATH); -d backgrounds it, --stop stops it, --tail prints a session's events. Needs the [serve] extra. Remote TUI tau --connect ADDR The TUI driving a session on a running daemon. The daemon builds sessions from its own config.json, so a client carries no store, keys or extension flags. Embedded (SDK) create_agent_session(...) in Python In-process, no subprocess boundary. tau_agent_core never imports tau_coding_agent, so this path has no Textual dependency at all.

tau -p and tau --mode rpc both write and resume real sessions — a headless run shows up in the TUI's session picker and can be picked up interactively later. There is no separate "headless-only" session format.

docs.title: Where sessions live
docs.text:
Default: <τ home>/sessions for the TUI and tau -p, where the τ home is $TAU_HOME (which must exist), else <$TAU_PORTABLE_BASE>/.tau if that directory exists, else ~/.tau; a private <tmp>/.tau-<uid>/sessions for --mode rpc (a subprocess a host spawns and tears down shouldn't litter the shared directory by default). --session-dir DIR overrides this for the file store. --store {file,jmfts} picks the backend for the run — ffwf-tau-jmfts is an optional package (pip install 'ffwf-tau-coding-agent[jmfts]'), loaded lazily only when selected, never a hard dependency of the TUI or CLI. --no-session skips persistence entirely (ephemeral).

A stored session has one writing process. Whatever hosts it takes an exclusive flock on a sidecar file and holds it until the last cursor on that session closes; a second process opening the same session gets a read-only replica whose writes raise, naming the holder. On a filesystem where flock excludes nothing (some NFS mounts) the session still opens for writing with a warning, which "sessions": {"allow_unlocked_fs": true} silences. Running a daemon (tau serve) is how several heads share one writer.

Sessions are append-only JSONL, walked by parent_id to build model input — not a flat chat log. That is what makes fork, branch, and rollback safe operations rather than special cases: AgentSession.submit()'s multitask_strategy="rollback" navigates back to the pre-turn leaf without deleting anything (the abandoned turn becomes a sibling branch), and multitask_strategy="fork" branches instead of extending the active leaf. See the Reference page for the full submission-strategy table.

tau --export-html REF [OUT] writes a saved session, every branch of it, as one self-contained HTML page: no script, a content-security policy that forbids fetches, and images inlined as data: URIs.

docs.title: Model credentials
docs.text:
~/.tau/config.json selects the default model (out of the box, a local-llm entry pointing at a local OpenAI-compatible server — vLLM, Ollama, or llama.cpp's server). τ never invents a credential. An environment key reaches only its own vendor's endpoint: a vendor's variable is not sent to a gateway on another host. The Anthropic and OpenAI wires send a request with no key and leave the refusal to the endpoint, whose 401 says which variable to set; the Google wire cannot, and raises (No API key for provider …). A 401 after a key was sent says where the key came from, and agent_end carries key_sent so a host can tell "no key" from "key refused".

A model entry names its vendor with backend and, optionally, its wire protocol with api. τ registers one vendor per protocol it implements:

backend api it implies Key read from openai (the default) openai-completions OPENAI_API_KEY anthropic anthropic-messages ANTHROPIC_API_KEY gemini google-generative-ai GEMINI_API_KEY, then GOOGLE_API_KEY

Resolution order for the wire is: a stated api wins, then the registered vendor's own protocol, then the openai-completions default. A stated api τ does not implement raises against the registry rather than falling through to the OpenAI wire — a model silently served over the wrong protocol is a failure that looks like a bad model rather than a bad config.

The two vendor SDKs are extras (ffwf-tau-llm[anthropic], ffwf-tau-llm[google]) and import on the first request rather than at module import, so a deployment that only talks to one vendor ships only that one.

An OpenAI-compatible vendor of your own — a gateway, a hosted inference service — needs no τ change and no extra: register a ProviderSpec at import time and point a model at it. See the Reference page.

docs.title: Retry, compaction and output caps
docs.text:
Defaults that changed since 0.10 and that an operator meets:

  • Provider retry is on. A request that failed before yielding anything is re-sent up to 3 times (about 1, 2 and 4 s, honouring Retry-After up to 60 s) on 408, 429, 502, 503, 504 and 529 and on a refused or reset connection. A failure after any output reached the caller is never retried.
  • Compaction is on in every head unless config.json says "compaction": {"auto": false}.
  • Output cap: a model entry that sets no max_tokens gets 32768. A completion cut off at the cap runs none of its tool calls and ends the turn.
  • --thinking off means off. It sends the wire's off form, or raises; an OpenAI-compatible model that cannot switch thinking off needs a thinking_level_map entry.

docs.title: Gateways that are not quite OpenAI-shaped
docs.text:
Two knobs cover this, both per model and both settable per call:

  • stream: false for a gateway that does not implement SSE.
  • request_timeout for one that is slow to first byte — it overrides the 300s read timeout and 10s connect timeout, which are otherwise fixed at client construction.

A tool call arriving with no name — a real defect on at least one hosted gateway, on some deployments behind it and not others — raises at the wire, naming the call id, the model and the base URL. The fault is the gateway's, and the raise says so instead of surfacing as a model that misbehaves.

Per-extension credentials follow the same shape: extensions.<name> in config.json, overridable per-run with --ext-config NAME:KEY=VALUE (CLI wins over config.json). An extension that needs a bearer token for a downstream service (JMFTS, a bus) reads it from api.config, not from an environment variable the model's own shell could printenv.

docs.title: Project context files
docs.text:
Discovery walks from the working directory to /, taking at most one file per directory. On a build agent or a shared host that means a CLAUDE.md in $HOME, or in a parent of the checkout, is read on every run. -nc (--no-context-files) turns discovery off, and it is run-level, so a mid-session model switch cannot hand the files back.

Two Fail-Early choices follow from τ's own rules rather than from pi's:

  • A file that is found but cannot be read or decoded raises, naming the path. A prompt silently missing its project instructions is indistinguishable from a model ignoring them.
  • Every block is wrapped in <project_instructions path="…">, so a prompt cannot carry instructions whose origin it does not state. If you are auditing what a run was told, the path is in the prompt.

The shipped default config carries no system_prompt key. Setting one replaces τ's base text and leaves context-file discovery alone — the two are independent, and a deployment that sets a prompt does not silently lose its AGENTS.md.

docs.title: Running as a subprocess (RPC)
docs.text:
--mode rpc gives a host process the properties a plain Python import cannot: a real hard kill. terminate()/kill() against a τ child works the same way it works against any subprocess — a runaway tool-call loop is stoppable from outside, not just cooperatively. The reader loop is strictly serial, so abort stays answerable while a turn is in flight (measured: get_state answered at +0.44s and abort at +0.46s against a 20-second provider call in flight). Embedding τ in-process trades this away — abort becomes cooperative only (each provider races its pending read against the abort signal, but a tool that never yields is not interrupted), and a wedged tool or a CPU-bound stretch shares the host's own event loop. Choose the RPC path over embedding whenever a runaway agent must not be able to degrade its host.

A host driving tau --mode rpc should call get_capabilities first (it publishes limits.max_request_line_bytes and the verb list) and give its own subprocess reader an 8 MiB+ line limit before it does — get_capabilities's own response is tens of kilobytes, well over the stdlib StreamReader default of 64 KiB. See docs/PI-RPC-REPLACEMENT.md in the source repo (a real integration writeup, not a design doc) for the full porting notes.

docs.title: Extensions in a deployment
docs.text:
Extensions that touch a message bus declare TOUCHES_BUS = True and are refused at load time unless the run explicitly opts in with --bus (CLI) or bus_available=True (SDK) — a capability grant, not a default. The declaration has a second half: such an extension must also declare a non-empty SUBJECTS, naming the subjects it touches. "Leave it unset" is refused even with --bus given, because the grant is per-subject rather than blanket. The shipped example is nats_bus.py (tau-006/tau-007), which needs pip install 'ffwf-tau-agent-core[bus]' for its NATS client: τ speaking NATS directly as a bus-native agent node, bridging to Tectum's effector nodes and to a simulation engine's world verbs. See docs/NATS-BUS-EXTENSION.md in the source repo for the full config surface and verb table.

Extensions come from three places: drop-ins in <τ home>/extensions/, installed Python packages that declare a tau.extensions entry point, and anything named with -e PATH or -e MODULE. Finding one does not load it: a discovered extension loads only once it is authorized (recorded in extension-authorizations.json beside the extensions directory), while an extension named on the command line is authorized by being named, so a headless host needs no approval step. tau ext list shows what is found and whether it would load without importing anything; tau ext authorize, revoke, disable and enable manage the records. An explicitly named extension whose setup raises fails startup. There is no project-local <cwd>/.tau/extensions/ discovery — deliberately deferred pending a trust gate, not an oversight.

docs.title: Testing without a live backend
docs.text: τ's own test suite points $TAU_HOME at a temporary directory (see tau_coding_agent.testing, which needs the [tui] extra, and tau_agent_core.testing) — a test that reads the real ~/.tau/config.json will happily talk to whatever real backend that config points at (a real JMFTS server, a real model endpoint), which is a slow and non-hermetic default worth guarding against explicitly in any Tau-embedding project's own test setup, not just Tau's.

docs.title: Dev loop
docs.text:
From a checkout of the source repo, rather than from PyPI:

python -m venv venv && source venv/bin/activate
pip install -e ./tau-llm -e './tau-agent-core[dev]' -e './tau-coding-agent[dev]' -e ./tau-jmfts   # Python 3.12+

pytest                # whole suite (config lives in the repo root pyproject.toml)
mypy tau-llm/src tau-agent-core/src tau-coding-agent/src tau-jmfts/src

The [dev] extras pull the TUI, REPL, serve, JMFTS, bus, images and code-mode extras transitively, so a plain editable install is not enough to run the suite. mypy takes all four source trees in one call — running it against a single package in isolation reports errors that are artefacts of the missing siblings.

A pre-commit hook hard-gates commits on the source repo over all five src trees — ruff check, ruff format --check, mypy, and a check that no multi-line comment block was added. git config core.hooksPath .githooks enables it locally; it requires the in-repo venv rather than falling back to a PATH ruff or mypy, because a different tool version passing locally and failing elsewhere is the failure the gate exists to prevent.

docs.title: Known gaps
docs.text:
• create_agent_session (the documented SDK entry point) is still not on the live TUI/headless path — tau_coding_agent's backend constructs AgentSession directly. The consequence that used to matter is gone: the backend now calls the same prompt builder rather than copying a config key past it, so τ's base prompt and its context files reach the model on every path. What remains is that the factory's other defaults are exercised only by SDK callers.
  • The reasoning level is no longer fixed per loop: AgentLoop re-reads model, key, reasoning and temperature before every request, and set_reasoning (RPC, /thinking in the TUI and REPL, ctx.set_reasoning in an extension) changes it mid-session. There is still no way back to "provider default" once a session has set a level.
  • There is no trust gate for project-local content: project prompt templates load unguarded and project skills are held back until one exists.

See the Reference page for exact signatures and the Cookbook for worked examples built from real code in the source tree.

docs.title: Tau 0.16 "Trusty" (preview)
docs.text:
Unreleased
